column1: 1|Shannon's introduction defines an engineering selection/reproduction problem and explicitly separates semantic meaning; the card attributes that framing and does not generalize the bit measure to personal significance. Base-two choice is a unit convention. The paper connection stays editorial.

2|RFC 1951 supports lossless reconstruction and the two mechanisms used in the example. The opening describes compression's purpose, not a promise that every input or short block shrinks. No lossy-reconstruction or universal compression-ratio claim is present.

3|The Huffman optimum is bounded to prefix codes for the specified alphabet and symbol frequencies, not every possible compressor or unknown future distribution. The codeword-boundary consequence assumes a valid encoded stream; the parent relation is specifically to prefix-free codes.

4|The non-prefix condition and sequential decoding are mathematical properties of a defined codebook. They do not promise synchronization after corruption or frame boundaries in an arbitrary bitstream. The relation to Huffman coding is an explicit example.

5|The description concerns canonical assignment from symbol-ordered code lengths, including equal-length lexical ordering. DEFLATE is named as the implementation example; no claim that all Huffman codebooks are canonical is made.

6|LZ77-style replacement is illustrated through DEFLATE's backward-distance/length format. The wording keeps that format attributed and does not equate every LZ77 variant's token layout or window policy with RFC 1951.

7|RFC 1951 defines DEFLATE as a format and permits fixed, dynamic and uncompressed blocks. The card retains all three, avoiding a claim that every block is Huffman-compressed or that Huffman alone accounts for repetition replacement.

8|Dynamic means a block carries its coding-table description before its content; it is not online rebuilding of the code tree after each symbol. Fixed blocks are contrasted at the format level, without claiming either always compresses better.

9|The Unicode annex distinguishes canonical and compatibility equivalence and the four forms. The card leaves recomposition conditional and avoids treating visual resemblance as equivalence. The standard's Unicode 18 revision stays in source metadata.

10|Precomposed/decomposed accents are an example of canonical equivalence, not a claim that all similar-looking strings are the same character. The relationship to normalization is editorial because it organizes learning rather than asserting an ontology edge.

11|The annex's circled-digit example and warning about mathematical/formatting distinctions bound the usefulness of compatibility normalization. The card says can help and may erase, without universalizing semantic equivalence.

12|The annex's concatenation table is a counterexample to closure under joining; the card says software can need renormalization, not that every join changes text. Boundary reordering/composition supplies the mechanism.

13|RFC 3629 permits one to four octets for scalar values, excludes surrogate code points, and preserves ASCII. The card correctly uses scalar values and separates assigned number from stored bytes; it does not promise one byte or code point per user-perceived character.

14|RFC 3629 treats overlong sequences as invalid and explains security consequences when validation and decoding differ. The card says accepting them can permit evasion, not that every decoder accepts them or every overlong sequence constitutes an exploit.

15|The numbered code space is distinct from UTF-8 octets. The scalar-value qualification avoids treating surrogate code points as valid encoded characters; byte counting is not asserted to equal grapheme counting.

16|UAX 29 explicitly calls clusters a best-effort approximation and discusses script, operation and font tailoring. Both approximation and tailoring remain visible; cursor movement is an example, not a mandatory behavior for every editor.

17|NIST defines sorted-input interval halving; SQLite's indexed row-lookup example supports logarithmic search effort. The card localizes that payoff to the SQLite example and does not claim logarithmic traversal cost for ordered linked lists.

18|SQLite's covering-index example contains all searched and returned columns. The card says the database can answer from it, preserving query dependence and avoiding a universal promise that every engine will choose an index-only plan.

19|The fruit/state example is explicitly SQLite-specific and demonstrates lexicographic column order. It does not assert that an index is useful for every predicate, that both orders are interchangeable, or that all engines implement the same plan.

20|The paper's date, selection/reproduction framing and logarithmic unit rationale are historical statements supported by the title/introduction. The wording does not attribute all later information theory to that paper or mistake meaning for its engineering quantity.

21|The replicated-state-machine example requires deterministic execution as well as a common command order. Add that condition explicitly so matching results do not appear to follow from ordering alone; the broad distributed-systems identity is unchanged.

22|Tables, indexes and transactions are illustrated by SQLite, rather than required of every database model. The wording does not turn a SQL example into a claim that all databases are relational or support identical transactional guarantees.

23|SQLite's overview explicitly describes SQL's declarative query semantics across implementations. Choosing among retrieval plans concerns result-equivalent query evaluation, not a claim that all SQL features are nonprocedural or that every query is optimized equally well.

24|The official SQLite description supports embedding without a separate server and a database occupying one file. The modal can avoids promising that live WAL mode has no auxiliary files; no cross-filesystem or unlimited-concurrency guarantee is made.

25|SQLite's power-loss atomicity depends on stated hardware, filesystem and flush assumptions. Add the documented-storage-assumptions qualification to the recovery example; all-or-nothing remains an observational transaction property, not simultaneous hardware writes.

26|The audit identifies a generic-WAL overreach. Keep rollback restoration but name SQLite's write-ahead-log mode in the contrast, retain later checkpointing in its evidence note, and avoid applying SQLite's preserved-main-file arrangement to every WAL system.

27|The first sentence currently defines WAL using SQLite's specific file arrangement. Name SQLite's WAL mode at the start and qualify the takeaway; append, commit marker, concurrent readers and later transfer then remain inside the documented implementation.

28|The SQLite read-transaction example is correctly scoped to WAL and a stable snapshot, with an explicit warning that visibility alone does not establish every system's serializability. No new claim about write-skew prevention is introduced.

29|Copying logged content back to the main file is SQLite's checkpoint mechanism; checkpoint meanings differ elsewhere. Name SQLite in the opening and takeaway, preserving automatic/application-controlled timing without suggesting a checkpoint on each commit.

30|The Raft paper explicitly requires deterministic state machines and common command order; both are present. Agreement is separated from execution, and no instantaneous equality of lagging replicas or Byzantine-failure tolerance is claimed.

31|Raft's leader, replication and safety decomposition is attributed to its design. Stops and disconnections describe crash/network faults, not malicious servers; agreement is not presented as uninterrupted availability under arbitrary partitions.

32|The selected identity is already bounded to replicated logs and crash faults. Make the majority-based safety/availability example expressly Raft-like so the source's practical-protocol description is not read as a theorem covering every conceivable consensus protocol.

33|Randomized timeouts reduce competing elections and retry after split votes; less likely and helps preserve probabilistic rather than guaranteed progress. Timing assumptions affect liveness, and no fixed election-time guarantee is asserted.

34|The extended Raft paper's joint configuration requires majorities of both old and new memberships. This describes that reconfiguration scheme rather than every implementation or one-server-at-a-time variant; the independent-decision safety rationale is preserved.

35|The replicated log is an ordered command history; the Raft example identifies leader propagation and committed entries. Deterministic execution is stated, and the card does not claim every follower has an identical complete log at every instant.

36|RFC 9110 restricts idempotence to intended effects and permits separate logging and different responses. Both qualifications survive; retry safety is about not multiplying the requested effect, not proof that every application implements its method correctly.

37|Entity tags are opaque validators; RFC 9110 permits different construction methods and strong/weak forms. The card avoids equating ETags with cryptographic hashes, uniqueness across all resources, or weak-validator suitability for If-Match.

38|The completed card already says an If-Match condition can require a matching tag. That leaves room for the wildcard existence check, and can stop an overwrite is appropriately conditional on the origin server evaluating the precondition.

39|RFC 5681's ACK-driven slow start and threshold rules support the description. Can expand quickly avoids asserting exact doubling every RTT despite delayed ACKs or implementation variation; no fixed numeric initial window is generalized.

40|RFC 5681 distinguishes congestion and receiver windows and uses their minimum. The card states an outstanding-data limit, not an estimate of actual available bandwidth or permission to ignore receiver flow control.

41|Saltzer and Schroeder discuss information protection and exceptional access paths. The card presents a design concern, not a guarantee of perfect security or a claim that access control exhausts all security objectives. Its mediation relation is directly sourced.

42|The cryptography card uses TLS as a concrete combination of confidentiality, authentication and integrity. Key secrecy is distinguished from secret mechanisms; no claim that encryption alone authenticates messages or that every cryptographic primitive needs a secret key is made.

43|Least privilege is a prescriptive design principle and damage-limitation rationale in the 1975 paper. The card does not promise that minimal permissions remove every attack or that permissions can never change when a job changes.

44|Permission-based default denial is the cited design rule. Tends to deny preserves the paper's failure-direction argument without claiming a flawed implementation must always fail securely or that missing configuration can never be exploitable.

45|Every protected access, including recovery and maintenance, matches the stated mediation principle. This is a requirement for a design, not an empirical claim that existing systems satisfy it; the source also permits carefully maintained cached checks.

46|Separating keys among authorities is a conditional protection design. Need not suffice retains the dependence on actual separation and enforcement, rather than promising immunity to collusion or simultaneous compromise. The comparison with least privilege stays editorial.

47|The paper separates mechanisms from keys/passwords. The card does not claim publishing a mechanism by itself makes it secure; examination without relying on secrecy is the narrower rationale, and the cryptography bridge remains editorial.

48|Small/simple design is motivated by detecting hidden access paths. The aim wording avoids treating code size as a measured guarantee of security or equating simplicity with the absence of necessary protections.

49|The capability glossary defines an unforgeable authorization ticket. The comparison concerns ticket-oriented versus object-list organization, without asserting that practical systems cannot combine both or that every possession token is a capability.

50|The list-oriented glossary supports associating principals with objects. Helps determine authority leaves room for other access conditions; the capability contrast does not imply every ACL implementation contains only one flat list or excludes delegation.

51|NIST distinguishes salt from hashing cost and requires collision-minimizing salts. Help prevent equal hashes correctly avoids claiming mathematical impossibility of collisions; offline password guessing is separate from encryption and online throttling.

52|NIST's throttling section allows waiting/disablement and recognizes malicious lockout. The card names online guessing and does not promise protection for an already stolen hash database, a universal threshold, or a frictionless control.

53|NIST's freshness requirement concerns replay of authenticator outputs even if transport is protected. Appropriately checked one-time outputs retains the verifier condition; passwords are correctly distinguished from protocols that wrap them in additional replay protection.

54|NIST specifically recognizes channel and verifier-name binding and rejects manually entered OTPs as phishing-resistant. The card concerns authentication-output relay, not immunity to every phishing consequence, malicious application, or compromised endpoint.

55|RFC 8446's public-key modes, PSK alternatives and early-data limitations are separately acknowledged. The card does not extend forward secrecy to every TLS 1.3 mode or claim that zero-RTT traffic has normal replay protection.

56|Appendix E bounds forward secrecy to later compromise of long-term material, with erased session secrets and appropriate modes. These conditions are present; there is no protection promised when the session key itself remains available or the endpoint is currently compromised.

57|Computer History Museum attributes early compiler and COBOL work to Hopper without sole-inventor or first-ever claims. The SQL comparison is explicitly editorial; it compares higher-level expression, not a documented claim that Hopper invented SQL.

58|The historical description supports the 1948 original, while object YS23/1998 is a working replica. Retain the explanatory URL and add the audit's exact context distinction in evidence/source metadata; no canonical identity equivalence between original and replica is asserted.

59|ENIAC's days of setup and approximate tube count concern documented historical configurations. Preserve could take and the initial-configuration relation; also clarify the Baby replica page used for that relationship so the original-machine comparison remains explicit.

60|The FBI's historical narrative supports 1988 disruption without the worm destroying files and the response-team consequence. Availability is the editorial lesson; no claim is made that all infected hardware survived unchanged or that this was the first malicious program ever.

61|The textbook's descriptive scientific goal does not establish that researchers lack biases. The card frames empirical study rather than moral prescriptions, and the impossible-word example concerns a language's pattern, not social judgments about its speakers.

62|The cited phonology chapter explicitly includes spoken and signed units and their patterned realization. The card does not reduce all phonology to speech sounds or claim that physical contrast necessarily changes meaning.

63|The cats and Inuktitut examples support word-internal composition and order constraints. Some languages qualifies sentence-like packing, and the card does not impose English space-separated spelling as a universal definition of a word.

64|The source explicitly extends minimal pairs to signed-language parameters. Qualify the card's sound-position definition as the spoken-language case, retaining the same general identity and the pill/kill example; lack of a found pair remains insufficient evidence of equivalence.

65|Atom/atomic is explicitly limited to many North American varieties and analyzed as realizations of /t/. Partly retains stress/context dependence without promising the same flap/aspiration pattern in every dialect or phonological environment.

66|The source treats complementary distribution as evidence needing further analysis, using /h/ and /ŋ/ for many English speakers. Both the dialect qualification and non-sufficiency remain; physical similarity is not presented as a universal mechanical identity test.

67|The a/an example is conditioned by following sound, not following letter, and plural variation includes predictable and lexical cases. Shared morpheme function is not equated with accidental resemblance between forms.

68|The Halq'eméylem claim is explicitly one reduplication pattern, and salad-salad is a contrasting English example. The card avoids assigning one universal meaning, such as plurality, to repetition across languages.

69|Replacement and movement are evidence for constituency, not a guaranteed algorithm for every construction. Can supply and complementary clues preserve the need to check grammaticality, intended meaning and language-specific patterns.

70|The telescope example holds the words fixed and varies phrase attachment. It illustrates structural rather than lexical ambiguity; the compositionality relation is an editorial connection, without claiming every ambiguity has exactly two readings.

71|The principle explains structured combination in sentences and multi-morpheme words. The card does not state that syntax alone determines all semantic properties or that every expression, including idioms, must be transparent from isolated pieces.

72|The sigh/breath example supports truth-conditional entailment and contradiction under denial. The explanation concerns the intended literal meanings in this example, not a rule that conversational inferences or presuppositions behave identically under every context.

73|The source's anger-versus-relief example demonstrates a cancellable contextual suggestion. The card calls it possible rather than necessary and does not equate conversational interpretation with mind-reading or a guaranteed emotional state.

74|Stopped charging backgrounds the prior charge in the source's example. The card avoids a universal claim that presuppositions cannot ever be challenged or cancelled; its point is taken-for-granted information versus the asserted change.

75|IPA is explicitly a speech-sound notation with broad/narrow choices. The card does not promise one unique symbol for every accent, represent signed-language articulation through ordinary IPA, or treat spelling as a dependable phonetic guide.

76|The source distinguishes stable variation from change in progress. The card retains that distinction and does not infer historical change merely from contemporary differences or portray changes as inevitable improvement or decline.

77|The method studies language in context, combining social and linguistic factors. May use retains within-speaker variability without implying all speakers or all variables show the same style pattern; social categories are analytical context rather than destiny.

78|The methods chapter describes a historical task sequence that can be tailored. The card explicitly states that not every interview needs every task, so reading/minimal-pair procedures are examples rather than requirements for signed-language or syntactic research.

79|Observation can alter self-monitoring and the source expressly denies a foolproof solution. Natural rapport helps but cannot guarantee preserves that limitation; the card does not treat all recordings as unusable or every observed difference as observer bias.

80|The source itself illustrates 10 versus 8 tokens with different opportunity denominators. The card accurately frames these as an example of proportions, not measured population rates or proof that a larger raw count always means more frequent use.

81|The methods chapter admits recorded speech, writing and interviews, then stresses representative sampling. The card says representation matters rather than assuming a corpus is automatically representative or that one person's speech establishes community rates.

82|The empirical example is Labov's New York casual-speech/reading comparison, explicitly named. The card draws a within-person variation lesson without asserting identical shifts across all languages, periods, variables or social classes.

83|The source defines above in terms of social awareness and describes prestigious external variants as typical. Often and the New York example preserve that distinction; above is not reduced to a mechanical upper-class origin rule.

84|The goose-fronting example is attributed to the textbook and Canadian English. Largely outside awareness does not mean every participant is forever unaware or that below-awareness changes lack social patterning.

85|The atlas passage records 1898–1901 fieldwork at hundreds of sites. The card stays historical, avoids the source's apparent personal-name typo, and treats map comparison as a learning method rather than a complete census of all French varieties.

86|The source attributes a Han-era compilation to Yang Xiong and distinguishes later dialect-group inference from the original record. The card preserves that inferential step rather than reporting reconstructed groupings as the author's direct field observations.

87|Labov's occupation/education/income measures belong to a particular 1966 New York study. The card presents them as research variables, not universal natural social classes or proof that income causes an individual's speech pattern.

88|The card explicitly attributes the account to Cenerini and preserves local histories, family legacies and Métis multilingualism. It does not treat all Métis communities as speaking Michif or present one practitioner's experience as a universal effectiveness trial.

89|The interview supports records of stories and family knowledge. Can preserve and may support avoid a guarantee that archives ensure intergenerational use; the comparison with reclamation is editorial and keeps the activities distinct.

90|The Michif case is explicitly attributed and the locally led scope is preserved. The claim concerns choosing goals with communities, not a single intervention that works identically everywhere or a broader language-revitalization synonym.

91|Peer Instruction is one inspected implementation of peer learning. Can expose gaps is a mechanism-based possibility, not a claim that every peer discussion corrects errors or that the cited course isolates discussion from all other teaching changes.

92|The IES guide presents retrieval as learning as well as measurement and emphasizes corrective feedback. Can strengthen avoids promising equal benefits for every test, learner or delay; closed-book retrieval is distinguished from restudy.

93|The guide's spacing recommendation relates useful delay to intended retention time. The card avoids a fixed optimal schedule and presents quizzes as one way to space re-exposure, without merging spacing with retrieval as an identity.

94|The interleaving example is restricted to the cited mathematics intervention's strategy-selection demand. The card asserts the task arrangement rather than an unsupported universal effect size, and does not infer that all subjects or novices benefit from maximum mixing.

95|Worked examples are described for beginners and the guidance amount changes with expertise. This preserves the guide's learner-condition boundary and avoids a rule that showing full solutions always improves advanced performance.

96|The guide explicitly describes retaining earlier steps and removing more later steps with expertise. The card describes that fading procedure, not every possible worked-example schedule, and does not guarantee successful independent transfer from fading alone.

97|The guide recommends explanatory graphics integrated with relevant verbal labels, and warns about distracting detail. The meaningful-integration condition is retained, so the card does not imply that adding any picture necessarily improves learning.

98|The cited recommendation connects concrete instances to abstract forms and discusses transfer limits of either alone. Can direct attention is appropriately conditional; the card does not promise automatic transfer merely from displaying several representations.

99|The guide's prequestioning recommendation draws mainly on reading studies and warns about selective attention to questioned material. The card retains its limited classroom-evidence qualification and does not turn the recommendation into a universal oral-teaching result.

100|The guide specifies cue-only delayed judgments rather than every delayed confidence procedure. Narrow the display label and opening to Cue-only delayed judgments of learning; preserve the reserved ID and historical label in metadata, with no new broader alias. Laboratory/classroom evidence limits remain.

101|The completed card describes producing causal/logical explanations and receiving guidance, consistent with IES Recommendation 7. It does not claim that mere repetition has no other learning value or that uncorrected self-explanations must be accurate.

102|CMU defines formative use by feedback purpose and explicitly allows later formative use of summative information. The card's final-exam example does not imply the exam was formative when administered or that every assessment necessarily changes teaching.

103|EEF distinguishes the original mastery model from newer variants and teaching for mastery. The card preserves flexible thresholds and organization, does not prescribe a universal 80% cutoff, and reports no average effect as a guarantee for every classroom.

104|The Mazur card attributes the sequence to reported introductory physics courses. It avoids sole-credit or universal-causal claims and does not treat gains in an evolving course as proof that discussion alone explains all improvement.

105|The source describes individual response, peer explanation, revote and instructor explanation. The card's focus is the protocol, not guaranteed correctness after discussion, and it does not require a particular voting technology or performance gain.

106|Scarcity, specialization and exchange are the textbook's introductory framework. Can increase production is conditional, and the card asks about institutions/information without presenting one economic school's policy judgments as established answers.

107|The used-car example concerns relevant transaction information and distinguishes unequal knowledge from uncertainty shared by both parties. The card does not assume all sellers know every defect or that all asymmetric transactions fail.

108|The insurance selection mechanism is conditional: a pooled premium may change buyer composition before behavior changes. It does not claim every insurance market collapses or generalize a jurisdiction-specific mandate as necessary policy.

109|Moral hazard is stated as an incentive mechanism after protection, with insurance as an example. May reduce incentive and imperfect monitoring preserve uncertainty; no clinical assertion that reduced health-care use is harmless is imported from the textbook's discussion.

110|Credentials are observable signals that may convey otherwise hidden qualities in the textbook's labor-market example. May and remaining uncertainty avoid claiming that a degree proves ability or that every credential is a costly separating signal.

111|Mechanic inspection and references are examples of information gathering by the less-informed side. The signaling contrast concerns initiative, not an exclusive taxonomy of every real hiring practice or a promise that screening removes uncertainty.

112|The reputation mechanism relies on repeat business and recommendations. Can and may keep the incentive contingent on future stakes; the card does not endorse the source's broader claim that cheaper sellers always imply greater risk.

113|The cited warranty promises repair/replacement under time and coverage terms. The card expressly depends on actual terms and does not create jurisdiction-independent legal entitlements, treat warranties as insurance, or guarantee seller solvency.

114|The risk-pooling explanation concerns aggregate funding of uncertain losses, with grouping and information qualifications. It does not assume all losses are independent, every pool is adequately funded, or that pooling removes every correlated catastrophe risk.

115|The textbook's actuarially fair benchmark equates premiums with expected group payouts. The card separates that benchmark from operating expenses and profit, avoiding a legal or moral claim that market prices must equal expected claims.

116|The deductible is presented as cost sharing under specified coverage, with its incentive effect attributed to the textbook's account. It does not prescribe a deductible amount or imply all services in every jurisdiction wait for the same threshold.

117|The supported sense is percentage cost sharing, contrasted with a fixed copayment and deductible threshold. Eighty percent is an explicit hypothetical policy example, not a universal coverage rate or a statement about other uses of coinsurance in insurance contracts.

118|Investor.gov supports the debt-security meaning, promised payments and default. Typically accommodates payment-structure variation, and the card explicitly separates repayment promises from guarantees; no investment recommendation or risk-free claim is made.

119|The price example specifies an older fixed-rate bond and resale, preserving the assumptions behind interest-rate sensitivity. It distinguishes issuer default and does not assert that every floating-rate, callable or inflation-linked instrument responds identically.

120|The coin jar is an idealized common-value example with differing estimates. Winning can reveal optimism rather than inevitably causing a loss, and the card does not confuse highest valuation with highest estimation error in all auction environments.

121|The Yale lecture presents private value as an idealized limiting case and housing as mixed. The card does not confuse private values with statistical independence between bidders or claim that all real consumer goods have purely private values.

122|The winner's-curse mechanism is selection among noisy estimates of a shared value. Can occur preserves the role of information and bidding behavior; no claim is made that every winner overpays after correctly conditioning on winning.

123|The first-price sealed-bid rule is described as a single-item format: private bids, highest bidder and own-bid payment. It does not import a general optimal shading formula or revenue-equivalence result without its assumptions.

124|The second-price payment rule and Vickrey name are directly stated by the lecture. The card deliberately does not generalize truthful-bidding incentives to common-value, collusive, multi-unit or other modified auctions.

125|The ascending format makes continued participation visible, and the lecture distinguishes its information from sealed bids. Can convey information preserves valuation-model dependence; the card does not promise exact equivalence to every second-price mechanism.

126|OpenStax distinguishes design decisions from a chart and explains information/resource coordination. The registered Organizational design ID and Organizational architecture alias remain preserved; the card does not claim a single optimal structure for all organizations.

127|Official reporting relationships are contrasted with actual consultation networks. May differ preserves overlap between formal and informal organization, avoiding the textbook's simplified implication that charts never describe actual work.

128|Emergent relationships can help or obstruct coordination in the cited text. Both directions remain, and the card does not reduce informal organization to friendships alone or imply that informal influence is invariably beneficial.

129|Mechanistic design is one anchor of a continuum. The card retains combinations with flexible elements and describes aims/features without promising that hierarchy or standardization always produces efficiency.

130|Organic structure is a flexible design orientation with distributed decisions. It remains distinct from merely having informal ties and does not claim that every volatile industry requires a pure organic structure or that formal rules disappear.

131|Functional grouping by expertise has specialization benefits and possible silo costs in the source. Can create and competing resources describe contingencies rather than inevitable failure of every functional organization.

132|Divisions organize functions around segments, with possible isolation and duplicated systems. Can and may retain the tradeoff's conditional character; the source is not used to declare divisional design superior in every market or company size.

133|Dual reporting is the matrix design feature, with possible conflicting demands. The card does not guarantee conflict or resolution by chart changes alone; the connection to organizational design concerns that specific coordination arrangement.

134|The approved networked-team sense is the task structure that develops after initial assignment. Flexible collaboration remains distinct from generic informal friendship, pure virtual geography, or a claim that all organizations naturally self-organize successfully.

135|The virtual-organization account is technology-dependent and permits dispersed/outsourced work. The card says can and may for benefits/risks, avoiding claims that every remote employee is isolated or that all virtual organizations have no physical base.
136|Span concerns direct reports and can accompany more hierarchy when narrowed. Can accompany avoids a deterministic equation between headcount and levels; no universally optimal ratio is asserted.

137|Formalization is the degree of explicit role/duty definition in the cited framework. The card does not equate loosely defined roles with no organization or assert that tighter formalization always improves accountability in practice.

138|CORE defines the principal-agent problem through conflicting interests and noncontractible action or attributes. The card preserves hidden attributes as well as effort and does not imply all employment motives are selfish or that one country's contract law governs the model.

139|Specification costs and verifiability are explanations of incomplete contracts in the source. Some and others preserve multiple causes; the card distinguishes analytical incompleteness from unsigned documents and does not offer jurisdiction-specific enforceability advice.

140|The card explicitly places effort and retention in the labor-discipline model and defines rent relative to a next-best alternative. Can influence avoids presenting dismissal fear as every worker's motive; no universal employment-law power to fire is asserted.

141|The labor-discipline model is named, with wages weighed against effective work. The card does not claim that any pay rise pays for itself, that all above-reservation wages have the same cause, or that efficiency wages are statutory minimum wages.

142|CORE distinguishes worker ownership/manager accountability from absence of hierarchy. Can choose permits governance variation; the card does not generalize one cooperative's profit formula or conflate every employee-shareholding arrangement with worker cooperative control.

143|ICA Principle 3 is a normative cooperative principle, not a universal legal dividend requirement. Proportionate member transactions and alternatives for surplus remain explicit. Its source record gains Principles 4/6 for another card, so this unchanged text still needs a reference-bundle version increment.

144|Toyota's account is attributed and the inventory/time goal is an aim. The card does not promise zero inventory, uninterrupted flow under shocks, or that all just-in-time variants use identical kanban procedures.

145|Toyota's explanation links automatic stopping to detecting abnormalities and less constant watching. Can reduce keeps the productivity implication conditional; no claim is made that every defect is detected or every production line achieves the stated ideal.

146|The Apple case is expressly historical and tied to The Economy's particular iPhone supply chain. The learning point distinguishes roles; it does not state current suppliers, present-day assembly locations or a current value-added percentage.

147|Foxconn's role is explicitly the historical textbook case. The card distinguishes contract assembly from every component and product ownership without claiming exclusive assembly today or making present labor-condition allegations.

148|L.L.Bean is an attributed textbook example of remote retail and reputation. The card expressly avoids a current returns-policy claim, so changes from lifetime to time-limited guarantees do not alter the stated learning point.

149|Federal Reserve History documents runs at trust companies largely outside clearing-house membership. Can grow bounds the institutional-boundary interpretation; the card does not claim one cause fully explains the panic or equate the 1907 regime with current banking regulation.

150|The source distinguishes inability to establish Knickerbocker's solvency quickly from proven insolvency and records suspension rather than permanent liquidation. The card preserves both distinctions and does not infer that every liquidity crisis deserves rescue.

151|The 1907 clearing-house account documents member loans/certificates and initial exclusion, followed by later aid. Initially is essential and retained; the card does not say trust companies never received assistance or describe today's institution and powers.

152|The conference and resulting exchange-rate system are historical, and the reconstruction bank is distinguished from IMF lending. The card does not claim every later World Bank Group body was founded at the meeting or imply immediate full convertibility for every participant in 1944.

153|The Bank's historical timeline supports private ownership, government finance and later nationalization. The coexistence lesson is limited to this documented institution, with no current legal-power, monetary-policy or officeholder claim.

154|The source reports limited trading, national-debt involvement and a share-price boom/crash. Tighten the closing interpretation to a direct comparison of share price and trading activity, avoiding an unsupported claim that the crash by itself established the company's intrinsic value or a single causal explanation.

155|ICA's history supports pooled resources, membership, democratic voice and custom-related profits. The card avoids claiming the first cooperative activity anywhere. Its unchanged text inherits a version increment because the shared principles source locator is corrected elsewhere.

156|The 1895 history supports initial information/principles/trade aims, while autonomy and international coordination are grounded specifically in ICA Principles 4 and 6. Correct the evidence and shared-source locators without adding membership counts or legal authority over every cooperative.

157|The bank's own account is identified as the source of collateral-free and village-center features; the 1983 transition is historical. The card expressly separates service design from demonstrated poverty impact and avoids current officeholder or borrower-count claims.

158|Toyota's official account is clearly attributed and presents a production-system model. The pairing of flow and abnormality response is supported; it is not treated as independent proof that every Toyota factory or product realizes those aims.

159|Toyota's historical narrative connects Sakichi's loom stopping to jidoka. The source attribution remains visible, and the card avoids asserting he invented all automation, proved a universal productivity effect, or directly designed modern vehicle systems.

160|Kiichiro's advocacy is separated from Toyota's later downstream-pull development after the war. The named historical account supports a coordination lesson without collapsing all later production-system changes into his personal invention.

161|The sociological lens connects interaction with broader patterns, and the role-conflict example is explicitly something that can be examined. It does not deny individual agency or claim one sociological interpretation is a proven cause of every work-family difficulty.

162|The network representation records actors and ties, with positions offering different opportunities. It does not equate a network graph with all social reality or infer that having a bridging position guarantees information or cooperation.

163|Easley and Kleinberg distinguish tie strength from local-bridge structure and qualify the job-lead argument. May and the explicit network-position caveat avoid claiming every weak tie provides novel information or every close friend is redundant.

164|Triadic closure is a tendency with opportunity/trust/context mechanisms, not a universal rule. The card expressly rejects guaranteed closure and does not confuse this empirical pattern with the separately idealized strong-triadic-closure property.

165|The local-bridge definition is precise for the chapter's undirected graph: no common neighbor, hence no alternative two-step path. If one exists correctly allows disconnection rather than promising a longer route always survives removal.

166|The structural-hole account is a theoretical opportunity argument with correlational studies and potential gatekeeping incentives. May and can preserve uncertainty; the card does not assert that brokerage causally guarantees promotion or that actors always deliberately preserve gaps.

167|The chapter's measure divides modeled flow among shortest paths; the card explicitly calls it a route model, not observed traffic. It avoids conflating shortest-path betweenness with degree, all kinds of centrality, or proven real-world control of messages.
